# How Veles found its canonical form

The ASCII form *veles* is not missing anything that this ​name requires. **Veles** is the canonical spelling supported by the Slavic transcription evidence and the tradition's scholarly conventions. This post explains what that form preserves, how it is pronounced, which narratives surround it, ‌and why consistency matters. There are no recovered accents to celebrate; there is something more useful — a spelling whose history can actually be checked.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Veles

## Overview

**Veles** (*veles*) — Cattle, Commerce, Underworld · Cattle god, possibly wool — belongs to ​the Slavic tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Cattle, Commerce, Underworld". The name means "Cattle god, possibly wool".

**Veles** — Volos to the East Slavs — is the god of cattle ​and wealth, of the underworld's moist depths, and, in the great reconstruction of Ivanov and Toporov, of poetry and magic. Where Perun strikes from above, Veles moves below: through herds, graves, bargains, ​and song.

## Mythology

The stories of Veles place cattle, commerce, underworld at the center of a living ​mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Veles appears in slavic tradition as cattle, commerce, underworld. The name's meaning, "Cattle god, possibly wool", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and ​later tradition-keepers preserved Veles in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Veles survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the ​interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration Veles ​gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

### Sworn by Volos (Oath-text)

The Rus'-Byzantine treaty of 944, copied into the Primary Chronicle, has left the only verbatim ritual text of ​pre-Christian Rus'. For the clauses of war the envoys swear by Perun; for everything touching livestock — sale, theft, compensation — they swear by Volos alone, and the curse on the perjurer is ‌total: 'may we be cursed by the god in whom we believe, by Perun and Volos, the furred one... may we not be protected by our shields, may we be slain by ​our own swords, may we be shot by our own arrows.' A later copyist glossed the unfamiliar name for his readers: 'Volos — that is, the cattle god.' The division of labor is ‌the myth in miniature: the sky-god witnesses between warriors, while the god of herds and wealth underwrites the peasant's entire fortune, animal by animal. Where your property lives, there your god is invoked.

### ​The Angry God of Suzdal (The Famine)

In the terrible famine year of 1024, the Primary Chronicle (s.a. 6532) tells how wandering sorcerers came to Suzdal' and announced the cause of the ‌people's misery: 'It is the god Veles who is angry.' The *volkhvy* demanded the sacrifice of a youth — a red-haired one, they specified, from a particular kin — and when the killing ​was done, they ate the body. The bishop of Rostov rode in, arrested the sorcerers, and drowned them in the Volga. The tale is told by Christian enemies, and its details are horrific ‌precisely in order to damn the old religion; yet its center is precious evidence. A generation after the baptism, when the official gods were Perun's rivals long drowned, it was still **Veles** whose ​name a prophet reached for when the earth would not feed her children. The underworld god was the one who explained hunger.

### The Theft of the Cattle (Reconstruction)

In the reconstruction of ‌Ivanov and Toporov, Slavic mythology's central cycle runs like this: Veles, dwelling in the underworld beneath the world-tree, commits a crime against the sky — he steals Perun's cattle, his treasure, sometimes his ​bride. Perun descends in pursuit, hurling his bolts; Veles transforms and wriggles — serpent, catfish, black eel — and each spring the thunderer strikes him down, and the rain returns to the herds. ​No East Slavic manuscript tells this story; it survives in the pairing of the gods in the treaty oaths, in wedding laments where the bride weeps for a brother struck or drowned, ‌in South Slavic spring songs, and in the universal Indo-European pattern of the storm-god and the serpent. The scholars who built it were explicit that they were reconstructing — and the pieces fit ‌with a stubbornness no rival hypothesis has matched.

- **Cattle horns** — The herds ​that were his treasure and the sign under which herders and merchants swore
- **The serpent** — His disguise in the myth-cycle: low, wet, and close to the earth — the eternal adversary of ‌the eagle

## Archaeology & Evidence

No ​monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to Veles with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Slavic name of this type the material record is ‌expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming ​Veles, sanctuary or cult remains tied to cattle and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before entering the ​scholarly record.

### Lord ​of Cattle

The chronicles gloss him explicitly: Volos, 'the cattle god' — herders swore their oaths by him alone.

### The Underworld River

He rules the wet, root-filled depths beneath the world-tree: the realm ‌of the dead and of hidden treasure.

In the reconstructed mythology he is patron of singers and sorcerers; the wandering volkhvy acted in his name.

### Adversary of Perun

The ​eternal enemy in the myth-cycle: thief of cattle, storm of wealth, struck down each spring by the thunderer's bolt.

## A Meditation

Veles is the god of the other economy. Perun owns everything visible ‌— the strike, the oath, the battle won — but Veles owns what accumulates quietly: calves, coins, verses, graves. He is the patron of everyone who works below the threshold of glory: the ​herder, the merchant, the poet, the sorcerer, the dead. His mythology, reconstructed stitch by stitch by modern scholars, tells of a being who is defeated every spring and never finally destroyed — which ​is exactly the biography of wealth, and of life itself returning from underground. There is something subversive in his survival. The chronicles drown his sorcerers in the Volga, demonize his name, and ‌reassign his cattle to Saint Blaise; and meanwhile ordinary Novgorodians keep doing business on his street, in writing, for centuries. Veles teaches that the underworld is not the opposite of prosperity but its ‌storehouse: everything valuable is buried for a season, and the god of the deep is the one who remembers where.
